detail:
NIDDK describes ulcerative colitis as a chronic inflammatory bowel disease in which abnormal reactions of the immune system cause inflammation and ulcers on the inner lining of the large intestine. Unlike Crohn's disease, it is limited to the colon and rectum and affects the inner lining continuously, rather than any part of the digestive tract in patches. Symptoms tend to develop over time and move between flares and remission.

Symptoms vary from person to person and can include diarrhea, often with blood, mucus, or pus in the stool, abdominal pain and cramping, an urgent need to have a bowel movement, and a feeling that the bowel has not emptied. More widespread symptoms can include fatigue, weight loss, anemia, and fever, and some people have joint, skin, or eye inflammation. Clinicians usually evaluate using history and exam, blood and stool tests, and endoscopy with biopsies of the colon lining, which helps confirm ulcerative colitis and distinguish it from Crohn's disease and infections.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about evaluation for ulcerative colitis symptoms.
sourceName: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
summary: NIDDK describes ulcerative colitis as a chronic inflammatory bowel disease limited to the inner lining of the large intestine, commonly causing bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and urgency, diagnosed with the help of endoscopy and biopsy.
takeaways: ulcerative colitis affects only the colon and rectum lining
symptoms can include bloody diarrhea, pain, and urgency
disease moves between flares and remission
endoscopy with biopsies helps confirm the diagnosis
title: Ulcerative colitis: inflammation of the colon lining
